$comment: FOUNDATION loop permissions. Committed and reviewable — changing what an
unattended session may do is a DIFF, not a keystroke.
ALLOW is scoped to what the RELAY queue actually needs: git/gh, the node
toolchain, the repo's own scripts, docker compose + exec (the QA stack and
read-only prod queries), and reads. It is broad within the repo and narrow
outside it.
⚠️ THE TWELVE SCRIPTS ARE ENUMERATED BY NAME, NEVER WILDCARDED. The first
version of this file said `Bash(bash scripts/:*)`. Two things were wrong
with it, and the second is the one to remember:
1. IT DID NOT GRANT. Session 01 measured the refusal with the sandbox
off, so it was the permission layer and not the sandbox. The loop
could build and gate an item but never ship one — deploy-prod.sh was
unreachable — and NOTHING SAID SO until a session tried to run one.
A grant that reads as present and is not is this file's failure mode.
2. HAD IT GRANTED, IT WOULD HAVE BEEN TOO BROAD. `scripts/` is writable
by the session, so a pattern matching any file under it grants
'write a script, then run it' — skip-permissions in two steps, and
every DENY entry below becomes advisory. Naming the files keeps
the deny list load-bearing. Adding another is a reviewable diff.
Per-script `:*` allows FLAGS on a named file (check-composite-fk --attempt)
without ever widening WHICH file runs.
⚠️ `cd`, `echo` and `printf` ARE GRANTED; `for`, `while` AND `$(…)` ARE NOT,
and that line is deliberate. A compound command is refused unless EVERY
sub-command is granted, so `cd X && <anything>` still needs a grant for
<anything> — which makes the three builtins cheap. A loop or a command
substitution is the opposite: its body is arbitrary text that no prefix
rule can bound, so granting `for` would grant whatever the body says.
A coverage audit of 114 commands the queue actually runs found 86 already
granted and 15 gaps, and MOST OF THE GAPS WERE THIS SHAPE — the capability
granted, the shell wrapper not. Their re-formulations are written down in
docs/foundation/MASTER.md so a session re-issues instead of halting.
⚠️ WHAT THIS FILE IS NOT: a sandbox. `Edit(//opt/meddoc-pro/**)` lets a
session change any file in the repo, INCLUDING the twelve scripts named
above — so enumerating them bounds what runs by ACCIDENT, not what a
determined session could arrange. The value is that widening stays a
reviewable diff and the deny list keeps meaning something. Stated plainly
because a permission file invites more confidence than it has earned.
⚠️ `Write(path)` RULES ARE NOT MATCHED BY FILE PERMISSION CHECKS — only
`Edit(path)` is, and it covers every file-editing tool including Write.
A `Write(//opt/meddoc-pro/**)` line sat here reading like a grant and
doing nothing. Same defect class as the one above: it was removed rather
than left as decoration.
DENY is the important half, and it is not a duplicate of the guardrails —
it is the mechanical backstop UNDER them. Each entry is something the
canon already forbids in words; these make the words unable to fail:
· force-push and history rewrite  — the 2026-07-27/28 purges
· deleting a pre-* rollback tag   — sacred by canon
· docker compose down / stop      — the prod stack, and co-tenants
· raw prisma migrate against prod — deploy-prod.sh is the only path
· nginx / systemctl on the host   — co-tenants share this ingress
· stripe live keys                — TEST MODE ONLY
⚠️ DENY BEATS ALLOW. A pattern here overrides any allow entry above, so a
broad allow cannot accidentally re-open one of these.
